# Railways (rails, flanged wheels, gauge) (`railway`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/navigation.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Navigation, transport & exploration (`navigation`)
- Deps: helped by puddling_wrought_iron, bessemer_steel, surveying_triangulation
- Core idea: Wheels running on smooth rails roll with very little friction, so one horse pulls about ten times as much on rails as on a road; flanged wheels on a fixed axle keep the wagon on the track. Lay rails to a constant gauge on sleepers and ballast, and keep gradients gentle (about 1 in 100 or less for locomotives), using cuttings, embankments and long curves. Wooden rails worn by iron wheels need iron strips, then cast and finally wrought-iron or steel rails.
- Pitfalls:
  - Steep gradients; smooth iron wheels slip on steep rails
  - Cast-iron rails for heavy locomotives; they are brittle and snap
  - Different gauges on connecting lines
- History: greece: c. 600 BC – Diolkos at Corinth, a paved trackway for hauling ships; europe: 16th c. – wooden mine wagonways in Central Europe (Agricola 1556); 1603–04 Wollaton wagonway, England; 1767 cast-iron rail plates at Coalbrookdale; 1820 Birkinshaw's wrought-iron rails; 1825 Stockton and Darlington; 1830 Liverpool and Manchester
- Read:
  - M. J. T. Lewis, Early Wooden Railways (1970)
  - Georgius Agricola, De re metallica (1556)
